articles.title_zh: San Antonio DJ heads to London for world finals
articles.content_orig:
by Yami Virgin, Photojournalist Paul Sanchez and Investigative Producer Natalie Medina
SAN ANTONIO — His dad, Rene Cardenas, is a famous San Antonio DJ now his son wants to take the city’s music scene international. Our Yami Virgin, who started out as a radio DJ while at UTSA, introduces us to an artist ready to make his own name on the world stage.
Two turntables, six minutes, and a chance to put San Antonio on the world stage.
"The DMC battle is the most prestigious DJ battle that has ever been on the planet," said Rene Cardenas, known as DJ RC3.
RC3 has won the U.S. Nationals.
Now, he's headed to London for the DMC World Finals.
"I'm going to go to London and show everybody how the USA Rolls and how we do it down here in the 210," Cardenas said.
He's competing in the classic category, showing off his scratching, beat juggling, and musical creativity.
Between practice sessions, he's studying business administration at St. Philip's College.
"I feel a lot more independent being that I'm really focusing on myself and I'm the one that's worried about myself and making sure that I am on top of everything," Cardenas said.
After competing in Tokyo last year, he says he's more comfortable taking the world stage.
"I make sure that I have fun while I'm doing anything related to DMC and especially when I'm out there," Cardenas said.
To help cover the trip, RC3 will showcase his battle routines at Pueblo Hall, Oct. 25, a chance for all of us in San Antonio to hear his skills before the world does.

articles.title_orig: World condemns deadly Houthi attack on Saudi Arabia’s Riyadh airport
articles.title_zh: World condemns deadly Houthi attack on Saudi Arabia’s Riyadh airport
articles.content_orig:
Riyadh airport attack was expected as the Houthis’ way to retaliate: Analysis
Saudi Arabia has accused Yemen’s Houthis of killing at least 12 people and wounding 300 others in a third attack on the Riyadh International Airport this week.
The victims on Saturday included four Saudis, two people from ⁠Bangladesh and one person each from the United States, Jordan, Palestine, Syria, Sudan and Egypt, the Saudi civil aviation authority said.
The attack was the deadliest in the kingdom in more than a decade.
It came as the war in Yemen intensifies, with the Houthis battling forces aligned with the internationally recognised government for control of the country. Saudi Arabia is waging an air campaign against the Houthis to support the ground war by the Yemeni government against the Iran-backed group.
Here’s a round of the global reaction:
US President Donald Trump described the attack as “terrible” and said he “will be speaking” with Saudi Arabia’s de facto leader, Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, soon. He also said he was evaluating whether the US should join the war against the Houthis.
“We may. We’re gonna look at it. We just found out about the recent attack, so we’ll make a decision. We’ll move very quickly,” he said.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, meanwhile, said the Houthi attack killed an American and called for an end to “these reprehensible attacks”.
“We stand with the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia and its people and extend our condolences to the victims and their families,” he wrote on X.
Hans Grundberg, the UN special envoy for Yemen, said the deadly strikes on civilian airports in Saudi Arabia represent “a grave escalation”.
“Such actions pose a serious threat to regional security, perpetuate cycles of violence and complicate even more peace efforts for Yemen,” he said in a statement.
The Egyptian Ministry of Foreign Affairs expressed its “strong condemnation” of the Houthi attacks, denouncing their “flagrant violation” of international law, and the “disregard” for the safety of citizens that they entail.
Qatar’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs condemned the Houthi attacks, describing them as a “serious violation of Saudi sovereignty and a direct threat to the security of the region, the safety of civilians, civil facilities and air navigation”.
It expressed its full solidarity with Saudi Arabia and said Doha supported “all legitimate measures” the kingdom “takes to preserve its sovereignty, security and safety of its territories”.
The Palestinian Ministry of Foreign Affairs declared “its full solidarity with the sisterly Kingdom of Saudi Arabia” and said it supported “all measures taken by the Kingdom to safeguard its security, sovereignty, and the safety of its citizens and residents”.
Japan’s embassy in Saudi Arabia strongly condemned the repeated attacks by the Houthis, saying assaults on civilians “cannot be tolerated” under any circumstances.

articles.title_orig: Man dies after entering tiger enclosure at England wildlife park
articles.title_zh: Man dies after entering tiger enclosure at England wildlife park
articles.content_orig:
Police say man was pronounced dead at the scene after being attacked by tiger
A man has died after being attacked by a tiger after jumping into its enclosure at a zoo in Yorkshire , police have said.
Emergency services were contacted shortly after 1.30pm on Saturday when the man entered the enclosure at Yorkshire Wildlife Park, near Doncaster , and was set upon by the tiger.
He was pronounced dead at the scene, South Yorkshire police said, adding his family had been informed.
Videos circulating online appear to show a man being pawed at and grappled by a tiger in an enclosure.
A police spokesperson said the tiger attacked the man and inflicted “serious injury”.
“Emergency services attended and sadly, despite the best efforts of medical personnel, the man was pronounced dead at the scene,” they added.
“Regarding rumours surrounding the condition of the tiger, the animal was uninjured and remained in the enclosure following the incident and there is no wider risk to the public.”
The force urged people not to share “distressing” video footage of the attack, circulating on social media.
Yorkshire Wildlife Park said a “serious incident” occurred inside the enclosure.
It said in a statement: “Our emergency response procedures were immediately activated, and emergency services are currently attending the scene.
“We are working closely with the authorities to ascertain exactly what happened.” It added that the “safety and wellbeing of visitors, staff and animals remain our highest priority”.
after newsletter promotion
Yorkshire Wildlife Park opened in 2009, with the Land of the Tigers attraction opening in 2011.
The attraction is on a purpose-built two-acre reserve for Amur tigers, an endangered subspecies with about 500 left in the wild.
Photos of the enclosure on the park’s website shows a high walkway for visitors and fencing above the section where the tigers can roam.
A Yorkshire ambulance service spokesperson said it sent a number of resources to the scene including two ambulances, Yorkshire air ambulance and a doctor.

A federal judge in California has sentenced a former Syrian prison warden to 60 years for torturing inmates and lying to immigration officials to get into the United States.
A jury convicted Samir Ousman Alsheikh, 74, in March of conspiracy to commit torture, three counts of torture, one count of visa fraud and one count of attempted naturalization fraud, according to the U.S. attorney’s office in Los Angeles.
Alsheikh was involved in torturing political dissidents to deter opposition to the regime of then-Syrian President Bashar Assad, according to the Justice Department.
Government officials say Alsheikh is the highest-ranking former member of the Assad regime to be tried and convicted in person outside Syria.
The Justice Department had sought no fewer than 80 years in prison, while Alsheikh requested five years, citing his age and his chronic medical conditions.
In handing down the sentence on Thursday, U.S. District Judge Hernán Vera remarked on the “utter reprehensibility” of Alsheikh’s crime, Courthouse News Service reported .
“The conduct was heinous, unimaginably cruel and unspeakably violent and brutal,” the judge reportedly said.
Nina Marino, Alsheikh’s attorney, said her client plans to appeal the sentence.
In a statement, First Assistant U.S. Atty. Bill Essayli said he hoped the sentence “gives some semblance of healing and closure to this defendant’s victims.”
“Criminals who inflict the type of savage brutality that this defendant did on his victims must never be granted refuge in our country,” Essayli said.
Samir Ousman Sheikh allegedly ordered inmates to a wing of a Syrian prison where they were then tortured with a device known as the ‘flying carpet.’
During Alsheikh’s trial, prosecutors presented evidence that Alsheikh ordered and participated in the torture of prisoners while he headed the Adra Prison, also known as Damascus Central Prison, from around 2005 to 2008.
Jurors heard testimony from three of Alsheikh’s victims who said they were packed into small, filthy, cold, wet cells that were infested with insects and other vermin. They described being tortured and seeing and hearing the torture of other prisoners.
The victims testified about being fastened to a device known as the “Flying Carpet,” which folded their bodies in half at the waist; about being manacled to the ceiling and suspended sometimes for days; and about being beaten while immobilized inside tires, according to the U.S. attorney’s office in L.A.
During the trial, prosecutors presented evidence that when detainees refused Alsheikh’s orders to harm political prisoners, he ordered them to be sent to an underground section of the prison known as Wing 13, where they were tortured.
Prosecutors also presented evidence that Alsheikh, who came to the country in 2020, lied to U.S. immigration authorities about his background to secure a green card and also on an application to naturalize as a U.S. citizen.
Alsheikh has been in custody since his arrest at Los Angeles International Airport in July 2024.
Khaled Abdul Malek, who testified about being detained and tortured under Alsheikh’s direction, praised the sentence in a statement .
“The land of freedom will never be a safe haven for slaughterers and those who committed crimes against humanity,” Malek said. “This trial is not the end, but the first step on the road toward accountability and justice for everyone whose hands have been stained with the blood of innocent people.”

articles.title_orig: US justice department investigates TV networks over Trump pool coverage
articles.title_zh: US justice department investigates TV networks over Trump pool coverage
articles.content_orig:
WASHINGTON — The Justice Department said it is investigating five major TV broadcast networks for potentially violating federal antitrust laws after the networks temporarily declined to provide pool coverage of President Donald Trump, a department spokesperson said.
The investigation into the networks that make up the White House TV press pool — NBC, ABC, CBS, CNN and Fox News — is underway, and the department sent out “civil investigative demands” on Friday, according to a Justice Department official.
“Members of the television press pool have boycotted covering White House events. Group boycotts among commercial competitors can violate the Sherman Act. The Antitrust Division is simply investigating to determine whether these news organizations have violated the antitrust laws,” department spokeswoman Emily Covington said Saturday.
The pool is a rotating group of networks that share duties of recording the president’s activities during public appearances and travel. The network performing pool duty then distributes information and media, such as video footage and audio, to other outlets.
The New York Times first reported the investigation.
The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
ABC News said it has not received any notification from the Justice Department but expects to. Representatives for NBC, CBS and CNN declined to comment. Fox did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
The investigation appears to be the latest move from the White House in its escalating feud against the press corps.
Last month, Trump barred CNN, MS Now and Politico from the White House grounds, citing what he said was “their constant ‘reporting’ FAKE NEWS!” The other networks in the TV pool briefly declined to participate in pool duties after CNN was removed from its spot in the rotation.
CNN, MS Now and Politico sued against the ban, claiming it was a violation of the First Amendment. They were reinstated about a week later after a judge ruled that the administration had to temporarily restore their access for 14 days. A federal judge this week extended the order to Tuesday.
The five major networks released a joint statement at the time, saying, “The public has a vital interest in receiving accurate, independent information about its government. No administration should restrict a news organization because it objects to its reporting.”
The pool system has been recognized by administrations from both parties for decades, and the coverage is used by pool members and subscribers, which includes outlets like Newsmax, One America News Network, C-SPAN and international outlets.
During the time the outlets declined to provide pool coverage, individual TV networks, including NBC News, continued to provide coverage of White House events that were open to the press, outside of the pool.
Bruce D. Brown, president of the Reporters Committee for Freedom of the Press, said in a statement that the First Amendment protects the decisions news organizations make about coverage, and called the investigation “another and even more brazen attempt to try to intimidate journalists.”
Kelly O’Donnell reported from Washington, and Marlene Lenthang from Los Angeles.

articles.title_orig: Back in Bushong: Brothers and World War II veterans Jay and William Moreland returned to their home and family eight decades after their deaths
articles.title_zh: Back in Bushong: Brothers and World War II veterans Jay and William Moreland returned to their home and family eight decades after their deaths
articles.content_orig:
The Moreland brothers have been returned home.
Repatriation activities took place Saturday afternoon for brothers Sgt. Jay Moreland and Staff Sgt. William Moreland of Bushong, beginning with a ceremony and presentation from the Morelands’ youngest brother, Larry Moreland, inside Robert’s-Blue-Barnett Funeral Home. Following the presentation, the brothers received a formal escort from Emporia to Bushong, where they were laid to rest with full military honors.
Following the ceremony, Larry Moreland spoke with KVOE News and said it was important to him and his family to hold a funeral ceremony for his brothers.
Moreland noted that he was, to an extent, surprised by the ceremony’s size and turnout.
The Moreland Brothers enlisted in the US Army in February 1943 and, at their request, trained and deployed together as members of the 149th Engineer Combat Battalion. The brothers died on June 6th, 1944, during the invasion of Omaha Beach on D-Day when their landing craft struck an underwater German mine.
Jay Moreland was 21 and William 19 at the time of their deaths. Larry Moreland, who was only an infant at the time of his siblings’ passing, says their military careers were indicative of how “inseparable” his brothers were throughout their lives.
As mentioned, Saturday’s ceremony was a largely attended affair by both residents and veterans, including a half-dozen chapters of the American Legion Riders who helped provide the brothers’ escort, alongside local law enforcement. American Legion Post 5 member Clay Childs says this turnout symbolizes the unity and camaraderie amongst military personnel regardless of their branch of service.
Saturday’s ceremony was the second repatriation ceremony for a native of Bushong after Sgt. John Owen Herrick was laid to rest back in 2024. Herrick was also a member of the 149th Engineer Combat Battalion and died aboard the same craft as the Moreland brothers in 1944.

Ukraine’s foreign minister says Volodymyr Zelenskyy has the backing of the Ukrainian people and deserves support , after Donald Trump called for Zelenskyy to be replaced as president. “He has the support of the Ukrainian people, and they have the right to decide,” Andriy Sybiga said on Saturday. “Statements from abroad only confirm that he is doing his job well. He deserves support.” Earlier, Trump said Ukraine needed “a new leader” a day after the US president struck a deal ​allowing Russia to supply diesel to global markets, and as Moscow launched strikes on Ukrainian civilians, killing 20 people including three children.
Trump on Saturday also called ⁠on Zelenskyy ⁠to stop hitting ​Russian ‌oil ‌refineries, saying: “He better damn ‌well stop.” Trump made the comments to reporters at the White House. Zelenskyy on Friday had reacted furiously to Trump’s deal with Putin, calling it “terrible” and “not fair and not honest”.
Further ratcheting up the tension, Trump said Vladimir Putin would like to reach a deal on the war with Ukraine , and without evidence accused Zelenskyy of resisting a compromise. “Russia would like to make a deal … but for whatever reason, Zelenskyy does not want to make a deal,” Trump told reporters. “President Putin would like to see a settlement, strongly,” Trump said of a phone conversation he had with the Russian leader on Friday.
The British prime minister, Andy Burnham, has moved to quickly back Zelenskyy , telling his Ukrainian counterpart they were in “complete solidarity”. In a call between the two leaders, Burnham told Zelenskyy he recognised that “the past 24 hours had been difficult for Ukraine and reiterated his complete solidarity”, according to a Downing Street readout. The leaders discussed “the importance of maintaining pressure on Russia”, with Burnham making it clear the UK “would continue to strengthen its sanctions on Russia and to take further action to constrain the Russian war machine”. They agreed to meet in person in the coming days, the readout added.
US ⁠negotiators Steve ⁠Witkoff ⁠and Jared Kushner, ​who have ⁠spearheaded efforts to ⁠broker ​a ‌Ukraine peace ‌agreement, ‌may visit Moscow within the next ‌two weeks , Russian state ​news ⁠reported ​on Saturday, ​citing ​a source.
A delegation of Ukrainian officials who visited Miami for talks on ending Russia’s war in Ukraine was on Saturday heading home , an aide to Zelenskyy said. “The groups are already on their way home,” Dmytro Lytvyn, an adviser to the president, told reporters.

articles.title_orig: Four dead and thousands without power after Hurricane Isaias lashes US
articles.title_zh: Four dead and thousands without power after Hurricane Isaias lashes US
articles.content_orig:
Four people have died and hundreds of thousands are without power after Hurricane Isaias battered parts of the southern US with powerful winds and heavy rain.
Officials reported two deaths each in the states of Alabama and Florida, which included people who were killed when trees fell on their houses.
An estimated 500,000 people in total were without power in several states as of Saturday evening, according to tracker PowerOutage.
Isaias made landfall in Florida late on Friday with maximum sustained winds of 105mph (168km/h) before being downgraded to a post-tropical cyclone.
The storm felled trees and ripped the roofs off buildings. Alabama, Florida and Georgia all declared states of emergency ahead of its arrival, while both Florida and Alabama issued mandatory evacuation orders to thousands of people.
Meanwhile, Hurricane Simon is bearing down on Mexico's Pacific coast and has strengthened to category four. It is expected to make landfall sometime overnight.
Tropical Storm Rachel, also in the Pacific Ocean, is expected to hit southern California later on Saturday.
Two deaths related to Isaias were reported in Florida's Escambia County. A woman was killed when a tree fell on her house, local Sheriff Chip Simmons said.
Joey Williams told NewsNation his wife had died in the storm. He said they went outside to snap pictures of the damage but, when they went back into their home, a tree fell through the roof and trapped them.
"I was able to squeeze out. My wife didn't make it," Williams told the outlet.
Simmons later reported that a man had died from carbon monoxide poisoning after running a generator in a garage that was not properly ventilated. Four other people who were in the same house were taken to hospital.
Officials had to rescue people in vehicles that became submerged by floodwaters. The Florida National Guard shared pictures of a truck stuck in a flood ditch, saying soldiers "stopped, swam to the vehicle and pulled its occupants to safety".
Florida Governor Ron DeSantis said flooding was a continued risk and warned of a "very hazardous situation".
In neighbouring Alabama, a sheriff was injured when a tree fell on him as he was responding to a car crash.
"Unfortunately, we have also learned that two Alabamians have lost their lives," Governor Kay Ivey said in a post on X, without giving further details on the circumstances of the deaths.
She also said officials were concerned about "spinoff tornadoes" in the state from the strong winds and heavy rain.
"As we approach the weekend and any travel plans, make sure you have reliable information as conditions develop," she said.
In Charleston, South Carolina, officials asked people to stay home on Saturday night as high tide is expected to reach 7.5ft (2.3m).
"After dark, floodwater is much harder to see and it's impossible to judge how deep it is from behind the wheel," the city said.
The storm is expected to continue to weaken as it travels to the north-east, but the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (Noaa) warned that the Carolinas and Georgia could see floods from up to 10 inches (25cm) of rainfall.
Hurricane Isaias was the first hurricane in the Atlantic's hurricane season, which largely has been delayed due to El Niño conditions in the Pacific.

articles.title_zh: What has Trump’s Board of Peace achieved in a year since Gaza ‘ceasefire’?
articles.content_orig:
It has been one year since United States President Donald Trump’s Board of Peace (BoP) brokered a “ceasefire” aimed at eventually ending Israel’s genocidal war in Gaza.
However, rather than receiving relief and a chance to rebuild, Palestinians in the enclave continue to face attacks and be uprooted as Israeli forces have expanded control within the territory.
Trump first proposed the BoP in September 2025, saying it would stabilise Gaza and ensure lasting peace.
In November, a United Nations Security Council resolution recognised the board as a “transitional administration” in Gaza.
But what has the board achieved? Here’s what we know:
The BoP’s mission was laid out in Trump’s 20-point Gaza peace plan , as was the “ceasefire” between Israel and Hamas. The ceasefire began on October 10, 2025.
The plan envisioned steps for each side to take that could eventually create a “credible pathway” to Palestinian statehood.
It required Israeli forces to withdraw to about 50 percent of the Gaza Strip and cease aerial and artillery bombardments. It also required Israel to release 250 Palestinian prisoners and another 1,700 people jailed from Gaza since October 7, 2023, the day that Hamas led attacks into southern Israel and Israel began the war. The plan proposed reopening border crossings to allow much-needed aid into Gaza.
The peace plan required Hamas to release all Israeli captives. It also proposed a later phase in which the group would disarm and its members would be granted amnesty or a safe exit from Gaza.
The peace plan established the BoP as a transitional governing body until the Palestinian Authority, which governs parts of the occupied West Bank, could take over.
An International Stabilization Force (ISF), led by the US, was supposed to take over security in Gaza from withdrawing Israeli forces, the plan stated. It also proposed the reconstruction and redevelopment of Gaza, whose people, it said, “have suffered enough”.
In February, the BoP’s members, who each joined in exchange for a $1bn annual fee, met in Washington, DC, for its first summit, at which member states pledged $7bn in funding although aid agencies said reconstructing Gaza would cost closer to $70bn.
On the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly in New York last month, the BoP also unveiled a 66-project recovery plan worth $2.4bn.
The BoP’s achievements are tied to the success of the Gaza peace plan.
Under that, Hamas has released all 168 living captives and Israel has freed Palestinian prisoners.
Hamas has also announced the dissolution of its government in the Gaza Strip although Israel has dismissed that as a “stunt”.
Other goals under the peace plan have been only partially met.
Governance has been hampered. While a National Committee for the Administration of Gaza (NCAG), meant to act as the governing authority in Gaza, was founded, Israel has not granted it entry into the Strip. The NCAG reports directly to the board and is led by Chief Commissioner Ali Shaath and other Palestinian technocrats. It operates from Cairo. Israel has not stated why the committee is not permitted to enter Gaza.
Aid remains restricted. About 227 aid trucks enter the Strip daily when 600 trucks were supposed to, according to the Integrated Food Security Phase Classification (IPC) hunger monitor.
Israel has classified thousands of basic items, such as tents and essential equipment like ventilators, as “dual use” items, which means they have military and civilian applications, and has restricted their flow into the Strip. About 1.4 million Palestinians – or most of Gaza’s more than 2 million people – will suffer hunger until at least December, the IPC has noted. That is 200,000 more than those who faced hunger in May, suggesting a significantly deteriorating situation.
Observers argued that the BoP has entirely failed to secure the “ceasefire” as Israeli attacks have continued almost daily on the Strip.
Since October 10, 2025, more than 1,400 Palestinians, mostly women and children, have been killed. In the three years since the war began, more than 74,000 Palestinians have been killed, and thousands more are missing and presumed dead under the rubble.
Israel says its continuing attacks target Hamas members, but the group vehemently denies the claims.
Israel also now occupies about 60 percent of the Strip, more than the 50 percent agreed in Trump’s peace plan. The “Yellow Line”, which demarcates the area of Gaza under Israeli occupation, has been pushed farther into the Strip, causing further displacement and squeezing Gaza’s population into an ever-shrinking area. Palestinians unknowingly crossing the “Yellow Line” have been shot dead.
In December, Israeli Defence Minister Israel Katz said the army “will never fully leave” the Strip.
Mohamad Elmasry at the Doha Institute of Graduate Studies told Al Jazeera that Israel is simply continuing a broader policy of “ethnic cleansing” in Gaza and the occupied West Bank. “They are making life miserable,” he said, adding: “This is all by design.”
Consequently, the BoP has also failed to ensure Hamas disarms so phase two of the peace plan could begin.
Although Hamas has agreed to hand its weapons over to the NCAG, it rejects the “disarmament” clause because Israel has not ceased its attacks or withdrawn from the Strip as agreed. At the same time, Israel has said it will not move forward with the plan if Hamas does not disarm, leaving the two sides in a standoff.
Meanwhile, no stabilisation force has been deployed. Six countries – Indonesia, Morocco, Kazakhstan, Albania, Kosovo and Uganda – have so far committed personnel to form a security force of 20,000 soldiers and 12,000 police headed by the US military’s Central Command (CENTCOM).
There has been no meaningful reconstruction in Gaza. Palestinians continue to live in tent camps infested with rodents and insects with little to shield them from intense heat, or rain.
The Trump administration and BoP have echoed Israel’s rejection of the United Nations agency for Palestinian refugees, or UNRWA, which has long provided lifesaving humanitarian aid, education, development programmes and social services in Gaza and employs about 11,000 Palestinians.
The BoP said last month that it will not work with UNRWA, essentially sidelining the agency.
A BoP official told The Associated Press news agency that UNRWA could continue working in Gaza if its programmes were deemed relevant but the agency’s “days are over”.
UNRWA said the move was “not logical”.
In June, the UN General Assembly voted overwhelmingly to extend UNRWA’s mandate until 2029. The BoP itself is mandated to oversee the peace process until December 2027 when its progress will be reviewed for possible renewal by the UN.
Analysts and rights groups have raised concerns that the BoP could take over all aspects of Gaza’s rebuilding. Countries too, including France and other European nations, have called out any attempts to replace the UN in the Strip.
But Elmasry said no country is willing to take action. “There are a lot of international actors that do not want to cross the US,” he said. That essentially leaves the fate of more than 2 million Palestinians to Trump, he added.
Ultimately, the BoP has “failed”, said Simon Mabon, a professor at Lancaster University.
“The failure to implement its own plan to end the Gaza conflict demonstrates its impotence and the inability to ensure that Israel and, to a lesser extent, Hamas, remain bound by their own commitments [and] has allowed the genocide to continue,” he concluded.

articles.title_orig: It's 'probably not plausible' that a strong economy can steady U.S. debt as 5%-6% growth is needed
articles.title_zh: It's 'probably not plausible' that a strong economy can steady U.S. debt as 5%-6% growth is needed
articles.content_orig:
Congressional Budget Office Director Phillip Swagel said faster economic growth is unlikely to keep U.S. debt in check, even if GDP expands at more than double its current pace.
Gross debt is now $40 trillion, and publicly held debt is 100% of GDP. Just keeping that ratio flat, let alone bringing it down, would require a massive, sustained boom. For now, CBO see the debt-to-GDP ratio soaring to 120% by 2036.
During a Minneapolis Fed conference on Thursday, Swagel said stronger economic growth will help by bringing in more revenue for the federal government, but it’s not that simple.
Federal spending also boosts growth, which lifts wages that in turn affect outlays on Social Security benefits, he pointed out. A robust economy also tends to send interest rates higher, which adds to debt interest costs.
“So growth will help, but it’s probably not plausible that growth alone will stabilize our fiscal trajectory,” Swagel added. “So then we’re left with changes in revenues and changes in spending, and those are inherently political choices.”
Minneapolis Fed President Neel Kashkari asked if AI can help supercharge economic growth, and he replied that CBO has detected an increase in total factor productivity, which measures the efficiency of labor, capital, and other inputs.
The CBO’s next batch of economic forecasts due early next year will incorporate its views on AI, Swagel said, adding that future growth will be stronger. Still, the budget deficit is so deep that even the extra AI-powered growth won’t be enough, he warned.
Kashkari then asked how much faster growth would have to be in order to stabilize the debt. Swagel cautioned against doing arithmetic on the fly but offered some back-of-the-envelope numbers.
Assuming interest rates of 4%-5%, he estimated that nominal GDP growth would have to reach 7%-8% and real GDP growth would have to hit 5%-6%.
That’s more than double the latest real GDP pace of 2.2% in the second quarter. Meanwhile, even bullish Wall Street forecasts put full-year GDP growth at 2.5%.
The rough numbers from the CBO chief also far exceed what Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said would be needed to overcome the debt.
“With 3% growth, we grow our way out of this,” he said at Southern Methodist University last month. “We’ll get to the other side of this Iran conflict, and the underlying economy is very, very strong, and I think reaccelerating.”
Meanwhile, other estimates fall somewhere in between. According to the Penn Wharton Budget Model, growth would have to average 3.5%-4% over a decade to maintain the debt-to-GDP ratio.
Swagel also noted that an economic shock that sends interest rates up suddenly would set off a vicious fiscal cycle.
“So there’s almost like a turbocharger,” he explained. “An interest rate shock feeds into the deficit, feeds into the debt, feeds back into interest rates.”
So far, the bond market is absorbing all the debt the U.S. Treasury is issuing to fund the budget deficit, but long-term yields have surged to the highest levels in 24 years.
Some of that is due to the strong economy, expectations for Fed rate hikes, high oil prices keeping inflation high, and the flood of AI hyperscaler debt competing for bond market demand.
But the enormous scale of U.S. debt is also a factor. Swagel said it’s small now, with a 1-percentage-point increase in the debt ratio leading to a 0.015-percentage-point hike on long-term interest rates.
“So it’s modest, but the fiscal trajectory is really quite challenging,” he added. “It adds up, and of course there’s that turbocharger type effect that I mentioned where it feeds back into deficits.”
Jason Ma is the weekend editor at Fortune , where he covers markets, the economy, finance, and housing.

articles.title_orig: WHO says no plague case registered after Russian lab worker’s death
articles.title_zh: WHO says no plague case registered after Russian lab worker’s death
articles.content_orig:
The World Health Organization (WHO) has said it still does not know what caused the pneumonia that killed a laboratory worker at a Russian plague research institute and that no case of plague has been registered.
Russia’s state health regulator told the WHO that tests on the worker and people who had been in contact with her were negative for the dangerous pathogens they tested for, the United Nations health agency said in a statement on Saturday.
Her contacts still showed no symptoms, and no further linked cases of severe pneumonia had been found, the WHO added.
“Based on the information provided… WHO has not identified evidence of ongoing transmission associated with this event. A key uncertainty remains the absence of a confirmed diagnosis in the deceased laboratory worker,” it said.
The worker fell ill and died in undisclosed circumstances on October 2, prompting authorities to quarantine about 200 people and stoking public health fears on social media.
Russian media named her as Darya Shipilova, a 28-year-old laboratory technician at the Irkutsk Antiplague Research Institute of Siberia and the Far East, in the Siberian region of Irkutsk.
Pneumonic plague, a lung infection caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis, which is usually found in small mammals and their fleas, was suspected early on.
The governor of neighbouring Buryatia said the woman had “died, maybe of the plague”.
Russia’s health watchdog Rospotrebnadzor said she had been diagnosed with “pneumonia of unknown aetiology”.
Russian authorities said the worker was appropriately vaccinated and that no microorganisms linked to her work were found in her body. They say post-mortem tests did not detect plague.
On Thursday, Russia said it had completed health checks on all her contacts and had given the WHO all the information.
A local official said on October 6 that 60 percent of those placed in quarantine had already been released.
WHO chief Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus asked Russia on Wednesday to respond to media reports of a second employee with pneumonia of undetermined cause. Russia dismissed the reports as “false information”.
The United States has also called on Russia for transparency.
Global health officials have been extra alert to deadly pneumonia cases of unknown cause since the COVID-19 pandemic, which began with a cluster of fast-spreading, fatal respiratory illness in China.
The cause of individual pneumonia cases often cannot be determined.

articles.title_orig: Christa Pike discharged from the hospital and back in prison
articles.title_zh: Christa Pike discharged from the hospital and back in prison
articles.content_orig:
This photo provided by the Tennessee Department of Correction shows Christa Pike on Jan. 12, 2023. Tennessee Department of Correction/AP hide caption
Christa Pike was released from a local hospital and is back in prison, at the Debra K. Johnson Rehabilitation Center in Tennessee, her attorneys Luke Ihnen, Randy Spivey, Stephen Ferrell and Kelly Gleason said in a statement on Saturday.
"She is grateful to the first responders and her medical team for their care in these extraordinary circumstances," the attorneys said.
They also said Pike is receiving medical care at the prison and they are tracking her recovery.
Pike had been hospitalized for several days after her botched execution last month, in which she received and survived two doses of the sedative pentobarbital.
NPR reported on the Sept. 30 execution attempt , in which Pike was strapped to a gurney and administered the barbiturate that is normally used in the U.S. executions. Shortly after the first dose was administered, Pike said her arm was burning and asked whether it was supposed to feel that way. She then said, "Please try up on my shoulder higher."
Spivey, who witnessed the execution attempt, previously told NPR that after a second dose Pike became unconscious but continued breathing and making choking sounds. "It "went on for so long," he said. He has called Pike "a survivor."
Judge I'Ashea Myles of the Davidson County Chancery Court in Nashville ordered the prison officials to preserve all evidence, such as messages, connected to Pike's failed execution.
Pike was on death row for a murder she committed when she was 18 years old. She and her boyfriend, Tadaryl Shipp, in 1995, tortured and killed 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer, a fellow classmate in the Knoxville Job Corps. Shipp received life in prison without parole for his part in the murder.
NPR's Scott Neuman contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: 9 dead, including children, in mass shooting in Erie, Pennsylvania
articles.title_zh: 9 dead, including children, in mass shooting in Erie, Pennsylvania
articles.content_orig:
Nine people, including children and a gunman, were killed in a mass shooting in Erie, Pennsylvania, officials said.
A man killed eight people including a pregnant woman, children and other relatives at his home in Erie, Pennsylvania, before taking his own life as well, authorities said Saturday.
Police first responded to a home on Perry Street in Erie on Friday, Oct. 9, around 5 p.m., after witnesses reported seeing a gunman firing shots outside the house before entering the residence.

When police arrived, they found two women who had been shot to death in the street.
The shooting escalated into a standoff as Erie Police and SWAT teams surrounded the home. More shots were then heard inside the home. When police entered, they found the bodies of seven other people, including children, as well as the gunman who died from what appeared to be a self-inflicted gunshot wound, according to investigators.
Erie Police Chief Rick Lorah described the incident as one of the most difficult and heartbreaking scenes he had ever encountered.
“The loss of life is devastating and the circumstances we are working through are deeply disturbing,” Chief Lorah said. “At this time, we can confirm that the suspect is deceased. Based on the information currently available to us, there is no ongoing threat to the public. Our hearts are with the victims, their families, and everyone affected by this tragedy. There are no words that can be adequately express the magnitude of the loss of life here.”
Investigators are currently working to determine what led to the shooting.

articles.title_zh: Tropical Storm Rachel's surf drives out Long Beach residents, briefly shuts Newport Beach beaches
articles.content_orig:
This is read by an automated voice. Please report any issues or inconsistencies here .
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
A coastal flood warning covered beaches from Malibu to San Diego on Saturday as Tropical Storm Rachel moved toward Southern California, while Long Beach kept some oceanfront residents under an evacuation order, and Newport Beach closed piers and temporarily shuttered beaches before a reopening.
“There is growing confidence that the expected coastal flooding impacts on Sunday morning for vulnerable south-facing beaches of LA County could be the most significant we have seen so far this season, including those seen with Marie,” the National Weather Service’s Oxnard office said Saturday.
Its San Diego office said Sunday morning would carry the highest flooding risks along the Orange and San Diego coasts as swells, onshore winds and high tides combine.
The center of Rachel was expected to move onshore in northern Baja California on Saturday night, the National Hurricane Center said.
Those warnings remained in effect even as Rachel’s forecast track shifted farther south, leaving most of San Diego County outside its projected path, said Adam Roser, lead meteorologist at the National Weather Service in San Diego. “Even though the track has shifted a little farther to the south, we’re still expecting wind impacts,” Roser said during a briefing.
A tropical storm watch remained in effect for all of San Diego County, the weather service said.
Long Beach’s mandatory order covers homes on Seaside Walk between 64th and 66th places. It took effect at 7 p.m. Friday and runs through noon Tuesday, city officials said. A commercial crane is scheduled to drop sandbags on 65th Place and westward in front of addresses between 65th and 64th, city officials said.
“The return date is subject to change based on evolving conditions,” a city announcement said.
Waves topped the bulkhead and sent water into homes and streets, according to city officials. Inspectors red-tagged eight buildings across 13 addresses, including apartments, and yellow-tagged at least one, Mayor Rex Richardson said Saturday. A red tag marks a building as unsafe to enter, and a yellow tag restricts its use.
The city closed the Peninsula to nonresident traffic, with more street closures starting at 62nd Place.
Richardson urged residents to “take this seriously and be prepared.” Todd Leland, a manager in the Long Beach Parks, Recreation and Marine Department, said the city’s bulkhead and pedestrian boardwalk had already sustained significant structural damage.
Workers are bracing damaged sections with timber and thousands of sandbags to stabilize the compromised areas and prevent collapse.
“Prepare right now for the impacts,” Richardson said. “Our infrastructure was not built for this.”
Long Beach City Manager Tom Modica said that he expected a lengthy recovery. “We will be asking for assistance from the governor, and potentially also from the federal government,” Modica said. “We don’t think this is just going to be this weekend. This is going to be the entire next couple of months.”
Water at the Los Angeles Harbor tide gauge peaked at 7.7 feet Saturday morning, about 1.6 feet above the predicted tide, the National Weather Service said. “The projected high tides of around 8 feet for Sunday morning would approach or exceed recent record tide levels for L.A. County,” it said.
In Newport Beach, police posted an alert online Saturday morning saying flooding closed all city beaches and piers until further notice.
“Stay away from these areas,” police said. The announcement followed Newport Beach declaring a local emergency Friday after overnight flooding on the Balboa Peninsula.
By early afternoon, police said the beaches were open, but Newport Pier, Balboa Pier and the Wedge, from the rock jetty to M Street, remained closed.
In a video uploaded to the city’s Instagram account, an official asked people to stay off the berms. The man said the flooding would continue over the next couple of days. “We want the public to be safe during this time. We will get through this,” his post said.
The weather service expects more coastal flooding Sunday, when high tide at Newport Beach is forecast to reach 7.6 feet at 9:48 a.m. “Low-lying property including homes, businesses, and some critical infrastructure may flood,” the agency’s San Diego office said. Surf could reach 6 to 9 feet, highest at south-facing beaches, especially in Orange County, Roser said.
Joe Angelo has lived in the Newport Beach area for 60 years and bought his beachfront home 27 years ago. He said the flooding left him in “shock and disbelief.”
“I haven’t seen one drop of water on that sand in 27 years. All the sand, not one drop of water,” Angelo said. “We all love living on this oceanfront. But, boy, it makes you think twice.”
Sandbags lined dozens of homes and businesses near Balboa Boulevard on Saturday morning. Beachgoers strolled with coffee in hand, went for morning runs and walked their dogs. Despite the warnings, many climbed sand berms to watch the waves. Some did backflips off the sand.
Chris Perkins of Orange County brought his son Connor to see the surf. “I grew up around the ocean, and [I’m] just trying to expose my kid to the gnarly waves, and show him how to be safe and how to do it the right way,” Perkins said.
In Long Beach, cars lined up Saturday at a Peninsula parking lot as fire department workers loaded sandbags into trunks. Light rain began falling shortly before noon.
Monica Shephard, who lives in a beachfront apartment complex, said she was worried, noting that ocean water reached her doorstep three years ago. She planned to pick up sandbags for her complex Saturday night and praised the city’s precautions. “They’re doing a great job,” she said.
Huntington Beach also activated its emergency operations center Friday, the city said. Many spectators watched pounding waves there at high tide Saturday morning. Cyclists, walkers and runners packed the white concrete trail along Bolsa Chica State Beach. A section that flooded Friday appeared to escape more trouble Saturday, despite signs that said “flooded.”
The heaviest rain is expected late Saturday night into Sunday morning, Roser said. Most coastal areas could get about an inch or a little less. Some mountain areas could get more than four inches.
Many areas west of the mountains will stay in the 60s on Monday, and Big Bear may only reach the 40s, Roser said. Temperatures should warm by the end of the week, he said.
Inland, southern San Bernardino County faces at least a 40% chance of excessive rain that could result in flash flooding through Saturday night, said Julie Phillipson, lead meteorologist at the National Weather Service in Las Vegas. “Our primary concern is still the heavy rains and the flooding that can occur.”

articles.title_orig: Hundreds of doctors demand World Medical Association suspend Israel
articles.title_zh: Hundreds of doctors demand World Medical Association suspend Israel
articles.content_orig:
Hundreds of doctors have gathered outside the World Medical Association (WMA) summit in the Netherlands, calling for the suspension of the Israeli Medical Association (IMA) from the grouping of physicians.
On Saturday, 81 healthcare workers removed their scrubs and hung them in a line facing the WMA assembly in Rotterdam, each bearing the name of a Palestinian healthcare worker currently held in illegal Israeli detention.
It was part of a protest against the continued membership of the Israeli association in the WMA, “despite them breaching almost every ethical principle in the WMA’s Code of Medical Ethics”, the IMA Out! coalition that organised the demonstration said in a statement.
“These scrubs should not be empty. Our colleagues belong with their patients, not in Israeli prisons. Today, we literally placed their names at the WMA’s doorstep,” said Mejrem Ahmetaj, a general practitioner and member of IMA Out!.
Since October 2023, Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza has killed more than 1,700 Palestinian healthcare workers and destroyed nearly all the hospitals and healthcare facilities in the enclave.
The campaign accused the Israeli medical association of remaining silent as Palestinian healthcare has been systematically destroyed.
“The IMA is not a bystander. It defends these attacks and blocks international condemnation while Palestinian healthcare is being destroyed. That is not medical neutrality. That is complicity,” added Ahmetaj.
At a meeting of international doctors, medical leaders and human rights activists during the WMA summit on Thursday, the destruction of Palestinian healthcare and the responsibility of the international medical community were discussed, the campaign said.
“Our Palestinian colleagues are being killed and imprisoned, where they are starved and tortured. Their hospitals have been destroyed and patients driven out or murdered. The IMA has said and done nothing about these war crimes against health workers, patients and hospitals,” said a statement by Jonathan Fluxman on behalf of IMA OUT!.
“Thirty years of WMA dialogue with the IMA has done nothing but give the IMA a sense of impunity … It is time for national medical associations and the WMA to speak out and take action. Break your ties with the IMA and suspend the IMA from the WMA now,” he added.
The IMA OUT! campaign said it delivered a petition calling for the IMA’s suspension, signed by more than 6,500 health workers from around the world.
They also demanded accountability for the complicity of Israeli doctors in the starvation, torture and medical neglect of Palestinian prisoners.
Among those held by Israel is Dr Hussam Abu Safia , head of Gaza’s Kamal Adwan Hospital, whose unlawful detention has prompted an international outcry.
He was briefly held at the notorious Sde Teiman detention camp and has been subject to torture and medical neglect. Doctors protesting in Rotterdam held up placards demanding his release.
Abu Safia’s son Elyas, addressing a meeting organised by the campaign, said, “My father and all Palestinian detainees must be treated in accordance with medical ethics, and doctors must abide by the Hippocratic oath they have taken. Care cannot be given based on whose life is deemed worthy.”

articles.title_orig: Protests against voter roll revisions rock capital of world's largest democracy
articles.title_zh: Protests against voter roll revisions rock capital of world's largest democracy
articles.content_orig:
Parts of the capital city of India, the world's largest democracy, are on lockdown. Protests over sweeping revisions to the voter rolls were met with a massive police crackdown.
Parts of the capital of the world's largest democracy are on lockdown tonight. Demonstrations flared across New Delhi today to protest a controversial revision of the country's electoral rolls. Authorities there have removed some 130 million names from voter lists or demanded more proof from residents to stay on the list. The protests took place despite authorities barricading routes and detaining hundreds of demonstrators.
NPR's Diaa Hadid is there, and she is on the line with us now. Talk about what sparked all of this - millions of names being struck off of voter rolls. How did this happen?
DIAA HADID, BYLINE: Yeah, it happened because last year, India's electoral commission announced it would clean up the country's voter rolls by removing people who died, moved addresses or were absent in general. And the ruling Hindu nationalist party, known as the BJP, also pitched it as an effort to root out illegal migrants who they claimed were on the voter rolls.
And there were about 980 million people on those rolls. This is the world's largest democracy. But through the role cleanup, an estimated 130 million names were struck off or were threatened with being removed. And one lawyer litigating against this special role revision is Kaustubh Chaturvedi.
KAUSTUBH CHATURVEDI: It's, by such a wide margin, the largest disenfranchisement that's ever occurred.
HADID: That's ever occurred - now, critics accuse the Hindu nationalist government of trying to disenfranchise India's Muslim minority and other groups unlikely to vote for the ruling party.
ROSE: And in the streets today, Diaa, did authorities try to stop people from protesting at all?
HADID: Yeah, they did. Security forces barricaded the area around the city's designated protest site. They cut off the internet in parts of the city. They even rigged up a loudspeaker blaring recorded warnings.
(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)
UNIDENTIFIED PERSON: Attention, please. Attention, please. Gathering here is not allowed.
HADID: So protesters, mostly young people, kept popping up in different places, and police kept detaining them. One outlet, the Indian Express, reported that some 6,000 people were detained in all. And they included protest leaders who were picked up from their airplane seats right after their flight landed. One lawyer we talked to, who was hiding in a courthouse, told us that dozens of his colleagues were taken away. The lawyer's name is Deepankur. He requested we don't use his family name for his own safety.
DEEPANKUR: I've never noticed such a large-scale detention of lawyers happening. It's unprecedented.
HADID: Unprecedented - that's a word we heard today a lot to describe the authorities' response. And at one intersection, we saw a rush of riot police blowing on whistles.
HADID: They were running towards a young man. It appears he'd shouted a slogan against the government.

HADID: Where are you taking him? Where are you taking him?

articles.title_orig: Care Starts Here: Self-care Strategies for World Mental Health Day
articles.title_zh: Care Starts Here: Self-care Strategies for World Mental Health Day
articles.content_orig:
Every year on Oct. 10, World Mental Health Day invites people around the globe to raise awareness, challenge stigma and advocate for stronger mental health supports. It is also an opportunity to pause and consider a simple but important question: What helps us care for our own mental wellbeing so we can keep showing up for ourselves and one another?
This year, the National Council for Mental Wellbeing is recognizing World Mental Health Day with the theme Care Starts Here . It is a reminder that self-care is not selfish or optional. Small, intentional acts of care can support our mental wellbeing, strengthen our resilience and help us be more present for the people and communities around us.
Mental health is essential to overall health, yet millions of people still face stigma and barriers to support. World Mental Health Day creates space for honest conversations about those challenges while reinforcing a shared truth: mental wellbeing is a collective responsibility. When individuals, workplaces, schools and communities prioritize mental health, they help create environments where people can seek support earlier and move toward recovery and wellbeing.
The observance also reminds us that awareness should lead to action. Action can include advocating for mental health services, checking in with someone we care about and building habits that support our own wellbeing. Care may begin with one person, one conversation or one manageable choice.
Self-care does not have to be elaborate, expensive or perfect. It looks different for everyone and may change from one day to the next. The National Council’s Care Starts Here self-care guide encourages people to begin with one action that feels manageable:
The goal is not to complete a checklist. It is to notice what you need, choose a realistic step and pay attention to how it affects you. A sustainable practice is flexible, connected to your routine and open to change when it no longer helps.
Mental Health First Aid (MHFA) teaches people how to identify, understand and respond to signs of mental health and substance use challenges. While learners build skills to support others, they also strengthen their ability to recognize when they may need care themselves.
Throughout MHFA training, learners practice approaching mental health conversations with empathy, listening without judgment and connecting people to appropriate support. Those same principles can inform self-care. Learners can pause to notice changes in their thoughts, feelings or behaviors; consider what support would be useful; use coping strategies that fit their needs; and reach out to trusted people or professionals when needed.
MHFA also emphasizes that supporting someone else does not mean carrying their experience alone. Setting boundaries , checking in with yourself after a difficult conversation and connecting with additional resources are responsible parts of offering support.
It’s important to remember that Mental Health First Aiders are not therapists, but a first line of defense — and self-care can help First Aiders protect their own wellbeing and continue to respond with compassion.
This World Mental Health Day, ask yourself: What do I need right now? Then choose one small step you can take today. Invite a friend, colleague or loved one to do the same. When we make care visible and approachable, we help build a culture in which tending to mental wellbeing is expected, supported and shared.
Care starts here — with a pause, a choice and the understanding that your mental wellbeing matters.
Self-care can support mental wellbeing, but it is not a substitute for professional care. If you are struggling, consider reaching out to a qualified health care professional or another trusted source of support.

If a mental health or substance use challenge is affecting you or someone you know, there are several resources available to learn more or get connected with help. If you are in crisis, or you know someone who is, contact the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline or dial 911 in case of emergency.

articles.title_orig: Man hospitalized after ICE driven vehicle strikes him during chase on Clay Road in northwest Harris County, HCSO says
articles.title_zh: Man hospitalized after ICE driven vehicle strikes him during chase on Clay Road in northwest Harris County, HCSO says
articles.content_orig:
HARRIS COUNTY, Texas (KTRK) -- Surveillance video obtained by ABC13 shows the moment an unmarked SUV carrying U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents ran over a man during a pursuit at a shopping center in west Harris County.
The video shows a white pickup truck stopping along Clay Road, facing oncoming traffic. Two men get out of the truck. One runs toward Highway 6, while the other, identified by ICE as Miguel Parra-Hernandez, runs through a shopping center parking lot.
Moments later, a dark, unmarked SUV turns into the parking lot and runs over Parra-Hernandez.
A witness who spoke with ABC13 on the condition of anonymity said he saw the incident unfold.
"He said, 'Ah! Ah! Ah! You broke my leg! You broke my leg!'" the witness recalled.
The video shows Parra-Hernandez remaining on the ground for several minutes after he was struck.
The footage also appears to show an ICE agent getting into the pickup truck Parra-Hernandez fled and moving it into the shopping center before leaving in another unmarked vehicle.
"I believe ICE agents moved it before we got there," HCSO Major Anthony McConnell said.
ABC13 reached out to an ICE spokesperson, who said agents were attempting to arrest the passenger, Jose Mendoza-Cervantes.
ICE alleges Mendoza-Cervantes entered the United States illegally from Mexico five times and had a final order of removal issued by a judge. The agency also alleges Parra-Hernandez is in the country illegally.
ICE said agents attempted to make the arrest and claimed Parra-Hernandez ran in front of their vehicle and was struck.
However, the surveillance video appears to show the SUV veering left through empty parking spaces before running over Parra-Hernandez.
A witness said the incident was deeply unsettling, adding that it could have happened to him.
The sheriff's office said ICE notified deputies that it needed emergency services following the crash.
HCSO deputies said their investigation would be limited to the crash, and they referred all questions related to the incidents leading up to it to ICE.
Mendoza-Cervantes remains at large, investigators said. Parra-Hernandez is in stable condition.
On Saturday, Harris County Attorney Abbie Kamin issued a statement regarding the incident, stating in part:
"Time is of the essence in getting the facts, and the public deserves clear, accurate answers.
ICE must cooperate fully with the local investigation. My office supports Sheriff Ed Gonzalez and District Attorney Sean Teare in their ongoing independent investigation, and the Harris County Attorney's Office stands ready to assist and support these critical efforts. We will continue to monitor developments closely as the facts become clear."

Apple revealed in a regulatory filing that it has reached an agreement to bring on team members and technology from personalized audio startup Huxe, in what’s commonly known as a reverse acqui-hire deal.
As first reported in MacRumors , Apple disclosed to the European Commission that it has agreed to make employment offers to “certain employees of Huxe AI,” and to “receive a non-exclusive license to Huxe’s intellectual property rights.”
Reverse acqui-hires emerged in recent years as a way for larger companies to hire key team members and license technology from startups without acquiring the startups outright — presumably allowing them to build up AI talent and tech without drawing as much antitrust scrutiny. (Confusingly, these deals have both been referred to as “reverse acqui-hires” and as plain old “acqui-hires.” )
In the case of Huxe, the startup was founded by developers who’d previously worked on the AI-generated podcast features in NotebookLM (recently renamed Gemini Notebook ). But Huxe announced on May 21 that it was shutting down , with the team posting on the Huxe website that the company would be removing its app from the Apple and Google stores, halting service, and deleting user data.
“The team is moving on to new things, and we won’t be continuing development of the product,” the company said. It also thanked its users, saying, “The fact that you used it, told friends about it, sent us your suggestions and your ideas, made it feel like we built it together.”
On June 9, shortly after Huxe’s announcement, Apple notified the European Commission of its deal.
The filing does not say who received employment offers or if they accepted. Nor does it disclose anything about Apple’s plans.
Possibly related: Huxe’s shutdown announcement came just a day after Spotify unveiled AI-powered podcast generation features of its own , so Apple could be hoping to add similar functionality to its Podcasts app. Tech executives seem enamored with the idea that personalized audio can replace regular podcasts (and maybe even parent-child interaction ?), though it’s not clear how many normal listeners agree.

articles.title_orig: Trump fumes at ‘stain’ on Norway after missing out on Nobel Peace Prize
articles.title_zh: Trump fumes at ‘stain’ on Norway after missing out on Nobel Peace Prize
articles.content_orig:
President complains about not winning prize in year he started war with Iran and says: ‘We will not forget, Norway’
Donald Trump complained on Friday about not winning the Nobel peace prize for 2026, a year in which he started a war with Iran .
At what was supposed to be a rally for other Republican candidates in Syracuse, New York, the US president devoted a long portion of his speech to airing his grievances with the Nobel committee.
“The United States of America, represented by me as your president, should have received the Nobel peace prize , but didn’t. And this is an indelible stain on the country of Norway, and those people that made such a disgraceful and embarrassing decision,” Trump said.
“The Nobel peace prize has been forever discredited by a handful of radical ideologues who are anti-democracy and really enemies of civilization,” Trump went on. “We will not forget, Norway , that you didn’t give this prize.”
Trump also recited a list of wars he claims to have settled, some of which were not wars and some that are still not settled, before adding: “I’m about to settle or win two more: Iran and Russia-Ukraine.”
Trump said he would be ending both wars “quickly”.
“I will tell you what,” he added, darkly. “Iran will be very quick one way or the other: that they give us everything or they don’t exist any longer.”
“Additionally, I stopped Iran from having a nuclear weapon and blowing up the entire Middle East and ultimately far beyond the Middle East, including Europe, perhaps the US and I saved more lives than anyone in history,” Trump claimed, despite the fact that US intelligence agencies reported to Congress in 2025 that Iran had actually suspended its pursuit of nuclear weapons in 2003.
“Despite all of this and all of these unbelievable accomplishments, the Nobel prize was given out today to a liberal person who works at the United Nations, who nobody has ever heard of,” Trump said of Navi Pillay , the South African former UN human rights chief who chaired the UN commission that concluded Israel was guilty of genocide in Gaza.
In Pillay’s first public comments after learning of the award, she joked to colleagues at a conference of human rights lawyers in Nuremberg, Germany, on Friday: “If you clap a little bit more, I may share this prize with Trump.” She then burst out laughing.

His opponent was Azerbaijan’s own Ushangi KOKAURI. With the crowd behind him, he had the chance to turn their energy into the biggest victory of his career. Every roar from the stands added pressure, but also belief that a home World title was possible.

articles.title_orig: Trump says he’ll decide whether to livestream the execution of Fort Hood shooter Nidal Hasan
articles.title_zh: Trump says he’ll decide whether to livestream the execution of Fort Hood shooter Nidal Hasan
articles.content_orig:
President Donald Trump said Saturday that he hasn’t yet made a final decision on whether to livestream the execution of former Army Maj. Nidal Hasan , who in 2009 killed 13 people at Fort Hood in Texas.
“There are two thoughts: don’t show it and show it. Cause you know, by showing it, maybe other people won’t be doing what he did. So I’ll make a decision ultimately. I know what the military would like to do, but I’ll make a decision,” the president told reporters at the White House.
He also spoke about Hasan’s crime, saying, “He’s a vicious killer — killed 13 people in cold blood, wounded over 20. Some of those people will never have their lives back in a true sense.”
Trump’s comments came a day after he told reporters that he “absolutely” approved the livestream plan announced earlier in the week, which has drawn skepticism and criticism from members of his own party.
Military officials said Monday that Hasan, who was sentenced to death in 2013, would be executed by firing squad in December. On Thursday, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said that the execution would be livestreamed , raising concerns that Hasan could be viewed as a martyr by others seeking to commit mass violence.
Trump says he’ll decide on Fort Hood execution livestream
But Vice President JD Vance said Friday that he was not sure the federal government would livestream the execution, adding that if it did he would not watch the event.
That same day, several Republican lawmakers expressed concern about the idea of publicly broadcasting the killing.
Rep. Austin Scott, R-Ga., wrote in a post on X, “I absolutely support the sentence of death, but live-streaming executions is what jihadists do. America is better than that.”
Rep. Rob Bresnahan, R-Pa., said in a separate post on X that “an execution shouldn’t be a live-streamed spectacle. The focus should be on justice for the victims and their families, not turning an execution into entertainment. Their pain deserves respect, not a public show.”
Rep. Tom Barrett, R-Mich., wrote on X that “Secretary Hegseth should seriously reconsider this decision.”
Other Republican lawmakers have signaled support for the livestream plan. On Saturday, Rep. Matt Van Epps, R-Tenn., told NBC News that “Parents should not let their kids watch that. Just like they should have good parental guidance for social media and other things. This administration is focused on accountability.”
Earlier in the day on Truth Social, Trump reposted a Dallas Morning News article in which Robert Jeffress, a prominent Trump ally and the senior pastor of First Baptist Dallas, said that he supports the plan for a public killing.

articles.title_orig: Abbas postpones Palestinian elections, sets presidential poll for September 2027
articles.title_zh: Abbas postpones Palestinian elections, sets presidential poll for September 2027
articles.content_orig:
President Mahmoud Abbas postponed what would have been the first Palestinian elections in nearly 20 years, issuing a decree on Friday to further delay voting for the Palestinian Legislative Council almost another year.
Rather than take place as scheduled next month, the decree pushes the elections back to Sept. 11, 2027, according to WAFA, the official Palestinian news agency. Presidential elections, which have not taken place for more than two decades, are scheduled for the same day.
The postponement leaves entrenched Palestinian leaders unchallenged and threatens to further erode the Palestinian Authority's credibility among ordinary Palestinians and donor countries who fund it.
The internationally backed body is dominated by Abbas' party, Fatah, and has administered semiautonomous parts of the Israeli-occupied West Bank since agreements reached in the 1990s. It has grown increasingly unpopular throughout Abbas' presidency. Many Palestinians view it as corrupt and criticize its security cooperation with Israel.
The decree came after a committee of top Palestinian officials met Saturday morning to discuss postponing the vote. The Palestine Liberation Organization's Executive Committee, which Abbas heads, said in a statement that conditions in East Jerusalem, the West Bank and the Gaza Strip were not conducive to holding elections, noting that Israel had not allowed election materials or international observers to enter Gaza.
The move was expected after Palestinian factions across the political spectrum met in Cairo for discussions on delaying the vote, Islamic Jihad deputy secretary-general Mohammed al-Hindi told The Associated Press earlier this week.
Palestinians have not held a legislative election since 2006, when Hamas won a majority of seats. Israel and Western countries then boycotted its government, fueling months of unrest that led to the Hamas takeover of Gaza the following year. Power has been divided between Gaza and the West Bank in the two decades since, with Hamas in control of Gaza and Abbas' Palestinian Authority in power in the West Bank.
The West Bank has grown increasingly violent in recent years as Israel has expanded settlements and outposts. Settler attacks on Palestinians and Israeli army raids on cities under the authority's control are both regularly reported.
Though the U.S.-brokered ceasefire plan reached last year outlined a future role for the authority, its immediate role was left mostly undefined as Hamas has continued to govern and the technocrats under the Board of Peace remain in Cairo awaiting permission to enter Gaza to transition power.
Before the postponement, leading factions had not registered slates to contest the election. But behind the scenes, veteran officials had been in talks to join forces and take aim at Abbas. An unlikely alliance had emerged between Hamas, Islamic Jihad and a bloc led by former Fatah security chief Mohammed Dahlan. Dahlan had previously been driven from Gaza by Hamas and was exiled in 2010 after a falling-out with Abbas.
"Abbas is terrified by the electoral alliance bringing our faction together with opposition factions and forces within Fatah that reject his leadership," Dimitri Dilliani, a spokesperson for Dahlan's faction, said in a statement.
Abbas has served as president since 2005 and delayed several presidential and legislative elections throughout his tenure.

articles.content_orig:
The Google TV Streamer is now well over 2 years old , if you can believe that. The streaming media box with its sleek pill-shaped design, was once the easiest recommendation in the business for someone looking to upgrade their not-that-smart smart TV.
But because we’ve reached the 2-year mark and Google handed the streamer a substantial price increase without any upgrades, there may be other options to explore before settling on Google’s box. You could also wait for a new model, which is reportedly in the works and has a handful of decent upgrades.
According to a report from 9to5Google , Google is working on the next-generation Google TV Streamer with several key improvements.
For one, the box will remain with a similar design, but Google is going to add microphones to it and also presence sensing. This should allow you to talk to it like a Google Home unit, but the presence sensing could aid in noticing your arrival in a room to showcase something like a Google Photos screensaver.
The new Google TV Streamer will reportedly gain a faster processor too, as well as more storage than the original, which only has 32GB.
Finally, we should see a new remote that will be similar yet include a couple of new shortcut buttons. The mini remote from the original Chromecast with Google TV was clearly not everyone’s favorite. While I’m not asking for a large remote, a few extra buttons and some additional length can go a long way in in-hand feel improvement.
What will the new Google TV Streamer cost and when might it launch? The report isn’t sure. That said, we do have some history to look at.
The Chromecast with Google TV 4K launched in 2020 . Google then gave us the HD version in 2022 before the Google TV Streamer hit store shelves in 2024. Google was on a 2-year TV product release cadence, but there are no signs of a new model launching before the end of 2026. I’d guess that 2027 could be the earliest we’ll see an updated Google TV Streamer.
Droid Life was started in 2009 and I can't believe we're still here. I've written over 20,000 stories on Android, reviewed thousands of devices, and still find some passion in a dying world of AI.
